titleStmt.title: Detecting Distributional Differences in Spatially Correlated Multivariate Data via Kernel-Smoothed Rank-Based Empirical Copula Tests

analytic.title: Detecting Distributional Differences in Spatially Correlated Multivariate Data via Kernel-Smoothed Rank-Based Empirical Copula Tests

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Comparing multivariate yield quality distributions across spatially referenced agricultural fields is complicated by two pervasive features: non-normality and spatial autocorrelation. Classical procedures such as ANOVA, MANOVA, and standard rank tests assume independence and therefore exhibit severe Type I error inflation when spatial dependence is present. We propose a nonparametric spatial Cramer-von Mises-type test based on kernel-smoothed empirical copula processes constructed from pooled componentwise ranks. Spatial kernel weights account explicitly for local dependence, while the rank transformation removes sensitivity to marginal distributional form.

Under fixed-domain infill asymptotics and polynomial α-mixing conditions, we establish weak convergence of the smoothed empirical copula process to a mean-zero Gaussian limit and show that the resulting quadratic test statistic converges to a weighted sum of chi-squared random variables restricted to the (K − 1)-dimensional contrast subspace. Practical inference is obtained through a Satterthwaite approximation calibrated using the exact discrete spatial covariance operator under a Gaussian copula model.

Monte Carlo experiments with bivariate log-normal spatial data demonstrate that the proposed test maintains nominal size across varying strengths of spatial dependence, in contrast to classical parametric and non-spatial rank-based methods, which become severely anticonservative. The procedure provides a theoretically justified and computationally tractable framework for comparing multivariate spatial yield distributions in precision agriculture and related applied settings.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Rigorous comparison of yield-quality distributions across agricultural fields or management zones is central to evidence-based decision-making in precision agriculture. Evaluating fertilizers, cultivars, irrigation regimes, or soil amendments requires determining whether observed differences in outcomes such as protein content, moisture, or nutrient density reflect genuine distributional changes rather than sampling variability. In practice, however, yield data are spatially indexed and rarely satisfy the independence and normality assumptions underlying classical inference procedures. Applying standard parametric tests without accounting for spatial structure risks misleading conclusions.

div.head: Challenges of Spatial Yield Data
div.p: Two structural features complicate inference for spatial yield measurements. First, non-normality is common. Empirical distributions of yield-quality metrics are often skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal due to localized environmental heterogeneity, including drainage patterns, pest infestations, soil variability, and microclimatic differences. Mean-based parametric procedures are sensitive to such departures from Gaussian assumptions, particularly in moderate sample sizes.

Second, spatial autocorrelation induces dependence among nearby observations. Measurements collected in close proximity tend to be more similar than those separated by larger distances. This spatial dependence effectively reduces the amount of independent information in the dataset. When ignored, it leads to underestimated variances, artificially narrow confidence intervals, and inflated Type I error rates. Empirical and theoretical work in spatial statistics and econometrics has documented that classical variance estimators can perform poorly under spatial dependence, motivating the development of spatially robust procedures [1,10].

Kernel-based smoothing methods have long been used to model spatially structured phenomena by replacing discrete observations with locally weighted averages that reflect spatial proximity [7,9]. While such approaches are typically employed for estimation and mapping, they also provide a natural mechanism for constructing spatially informed test statistics. At the same time, rank-based procedures offer robustness to skewness and heavy tails by relying on order information rather than moment assumptions [3]. Integrating these two ideas suggests a framework for distributional comparison that is both robust to non-normality and explicitly attentive to spatial geometry.

div.head: Limitations of Classical Tests Under Spatial Dependence
div.p: Standard inferential tools such as the t-test, ANOVA, and MANOVA assume independent observations and often approximate normality. When applied to spatially correlated yield data, these methods typically underestimate sampling variability. In agricultural applications, this can produce spurious declarations of statistically significant differences between fields or management zones. Even nonparametric rank tests, while robust to non-normality, generally retain an implicit independence assumption and therefore remain vulnerable to spatial variance inflation.

Spatially robust covariance estimators and heteroskedasticity-and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) methods address some aspects of dependence [1]. However, they are usually formulated for mean-based statistics rather than full distributional comparison. Geostatistical approaches such as kriging focus primarily on prediction and spatial interpolation rather than formal hypothesis testing of equality of distributions [7]. Consequently, there remains a methodological gap for tests that (i) compare entire yield-quality distributions, (ii) remain robust to heavy tails and outliers, and (iii) accommodate spatial dependence in a theoretically principled manner.

div.head: A Rank-Based Spatial Testing Framework
div.p: We propose a spatial Cramer-von Mises-type testing procedure built on kernel-smoothed empirical distribution functions (EDFs) constructed from pooled ranks. The approach combines three elements.

First, rank transformation reduces sensitivity to skewness and extreme observations by replacing raw measurements with their relative ordering within the pooled sample. This yields a distribution-free representation under the null hypothesis and avoids reliance on moment conditions.

Second, spatial kernel smoothing incorporates the geometry of observation locations. By weighting observations according to spatial proximity to a reference location, the resulting smoothed EDF reflects local spatial structure while preserving distributional information. The effective sample size is determined by the kernel weights, providing a transparent link between spatial dependence and variance inflation.

Third, under α-mixing (strong mixing) conditions that quantify the decay of spatial dependence, we establish that the normalized contrast process converges weakly to a mean-zero Gaussian limit. The associated quadratic test statistic converges in distribution to a weighted sum of chi-squared random variables, with eigenvalues determined by the spatial covariance operator induced by the kernel and the dependence structure. This limiting form enables direct p-value computation without intensive resampling.

For practical implementation, we approximate the weighted chi-squared limit using a Satterthwaite-type moment-matching approach. The required eigenvalues are obtained from an exact discrete covariance operator evaluated on a finite grid, yielding a computationally tractable procedure suitable for routine agronomic datasets.

div.head: Scope and Contributions
div.p: The proposed framework targets comparison of yield-quality distributions across multiple fields or management zones and extends naturally to multivariate outcomes. By focusing on distributional equality rather than mean differences alone, the method complements existing geostatistical smoothing techniques that emphasize prediction or interpolation. Theoretical guarantees under spatial mixing conditions provide a rigorous foundation, while simulation studies demonstrate that the procedure maintains nominal size in settings where classical parametric and non-spatial rank-based tests exhibit severe size distortions. Together, these elements form a coherent and practically implementable approach to distributional inference for spatially dependent agricultural data.

div.head: Statistical Model and Notation
div.p: Let there be K fields indexed by k = 1, . . . , K. For field k, observations are collected on a regular lattice L n,k = {s k1 , . . . , s kn k } ⊂ D k with mesh ∆ n → 0. Thus n k → ∞ and D k ⊂ R 2 is fixed and bounded.
The yield quality observed at location s kj is X k,s kj . Within each field, {X k,s : s ∈ R 2 } is assumed strictly stationary and isotropic with marginal CDF F k .
The hypothesis of interest is:
div.formula: H 0 : F 1 (x) = F 2 (x) = • • • = F K (x) = F (x) ∀x ∈ R Spatial dependence.
div.p: For each field k, let α k (r) be the α-mixing coefficient. We assume polynomial decay: Assumption 1 (α-mixing decay). There exist constants C > 0, θ > 4 such that α k (r) ≤ Cr −θ for all r ≥ 0 and all k.
This rate implies absolute integrability of the relevant covariance functions via Davydov's inequality, ensuring central limit behavior for local (kernel-weighted) averages.

div.head: Kernel-Smoothed Empirical Distribution Function
div.p: Fix an interior reference location s 0 . Let K : R 2 → R be bounded, symmetric, Lipschitz, compactly supported, and satisfy R 2 K(u)du = 1. For a fixed bandwidth h > 0, define K h (u) = h −2 K(u/h) and the smoothed EDF:
div.formula: Fk,h (x; s 0 ) = n k j=1 K h (s kj − s 0 )1{X k,s kj ≤ x} n k j=1 K h (s kj − s 0 )
div.p: Because the design is deterministic, the effective local sample size is determined by the normalized weights W j = K h (s kj − s 0 )/ K h (s kj − s 0 ), giving an exact finite-sample effective size of:
div.formula: m n,k := 1 n k j=1 W 2 j
div.p: Under a regular lattice and regular kernel, m n,k ≍ h 2 /∆ 2 n , so this scaling aligns with the infill asymptotic regime. Accordingly, we work with the normalized empirical process:
div.formula: Gn,k (x) := √ m n,k ( Fk,h (x; s 0 ) − F (x))

div.head: Contrast Processes and Test Statistic
div.p: Let m n := K k=1 m n,k . Define the pooled smoothed EDF using effective sample size weights:
div.formula: Fh (x; s 0 ) := K k=1 m n,k m n Fk,h (x; s 0 )
div.p: The natural scaling for differences is √ m n . Define the contrast processes:
div.formula: Hn,k (x) := √ m n ( Fk,h (x; s 0 ) − Fh (x; s 0 ))
div.p: We use an L 2 (F )-type quadratic form test statistic, evaluated over M discrete thresholds. In practice, this is computed as a weighted Riemann sum over intervals ∆ Fh (x i ). To connect with the discrete implementation, we define a discretized inner product on the grid {x 1 , . . . , x M } with weights w i approximating dF (e.g., w i = ∆ Fh (x i )). Then
div.formula: T n := 1 K K k=1 M i=1 [ Hn,k (x i )] 2 w i .
div.p: This corresponds to the squared norm of the K-variate contrast vector in the discretized space, with the factor 1/K ensuring an average over fields. The asymptotic eigenvalues λ m are then scaled appropriately when matching the Satterthwaite approximation to the discretized statistic.

div.head: Practical Inference via the Satterthwaite Approximation
div.p: Because Hn,k is a linear transformation of the fieldwise processes, its limiting covariance operator is obtained by applying the same linear transformation at the Gaussian-process limit level. T n converges to a weighted sum of chisquared variables with K − 1 degrees of freedom for each eigen-component (reflecting the contrast subspace). Specifically,
div.formula: T n d − → ∞ m=1 λ m χ 2 K−1,m ,
div.p: where {λ m } are the nonzero eigenvalues of the covariance operator restricted to the contrast subspace, and χ 2 K−1,m are independent chi-square variables with K − 1 degrees of freedom.
We approximate this mixture by a single aχ 2 ν (Satterthwaite) by matching the first two moments using estimated eigenvalues:
div.formula: a = λ 2 m λ m , ν = ( λ m ) 2 λ 2 m .

div.head: Multivariate Extension
div.p: The framework naturally extends to comparing joint probability distributions of p distinct agricultural characteristics (e.g., simultaneously analyzing protein content and test weight). For a p-dimensional quality vector X k,s = (X (1) , X (2) , . . . , X (p) ), the smoothed EDF evaluates the joint indicator function 1{X k,s kj ≤ x} over a multivariate grid x ∈ R p . Under a Gaussian copula model for the dependence structure, the covariance between indicators at two spatial locations s and t involves a 4pdimensional multivariate normal probability (because we consider both variables at both sites). For p = 2 this reduces to a 4-dimensional calculation, which our code implements. The test statistic averages over an M p grid, and the same weighted chi-square asymptotics hold.

div.head: Mathematical Framework and Asymptotic Theory
div.p: For the theoretical development we specialize to d = 2 dimensions throughout. All integrals are over R 2 .

Lemma 1 (Asymptotic covariance under fixed-bandwidth infill). Assume H 0 so that F k ≡ F and assume the field {X k,s } is strictly stationary and α-mixing with α(r) ≤ Cr −θ for some θ > 2(2 + δ)/δ and some δ > 0. For fixed x, y ∈ R,
div.formula: lim n→∞ Cov Gn,k (x), Gn,k (y) = R 2 γ k (t; x, y)ψ h (t)dt
div.p: where
div.formula: γ k (t; x, y) = Cov 1{X k,0 ≤ x}, 1{X k,t ≤ y} , ψ h (t) := R 2 K h (u)K h (u − t)du.
div.p: The integral converges absolutely.
div.formula: Theorem 1 (Weak convergence of Gn,k ). Under Assumption 1, Gn,k ⇒ G k in ℓ ∞ (R)
div.p: , where G k is a mean-zero Gaussian process with covariance Γ k (x, y) given by Lemma 1. If fields are observed on independent domains, then (G 1 , . . . , G K ) are independent.

Theorem 2 (Asymptotic null distribution). Under H 0 and Assumption 1, the test statistic converges in distribution to a weighted sum of independent chi-square random variables with K − 1 degrees of freedom:
div.formula: T n d − → ∞ m=1 λ m χ 2 K−1,m ,
div.p: where {λ m } are the nonzero eigenvalues of the covariance operator restricted to the (K − 1)-dimensional contrast subspace.

div.head: Simulation Study
div.p: We conducted Monte Carlo experiments to evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed Spatial-CvM test in both univariate and multivariate settings. Data was simulated across K = 3 fields on a 20 × 20 grid covering the unit square.

div.head: Design
div.p: The latent Gaussian random fields have an exponential correlation function Corr(Z k (s), Z k (t)) = exp(−∥s−t∥/ϕ) where ϕ ∈ {0.01, 0.20, 0.50}. Observed yields are strictly positive and skewed via the log-normal transformation Y k (s) = exp(Z k (s)). We evaluate Type I error rate (Size) under the null, and Power under a multiplicative location shift δ.

div.head: Univariate Results
div.p: Table 1 demonstrates the empirical Type I error rate. The Spatial-CvM test successfully controls the false positive rate, achieving values close to the nominal 0.05 level when fields are nearly independent (ϕ = 0.01), and maintaining strong control under moderate dependence (ϕ = 0.20). In stark contrast, naive tests like Kruskal-Wallis (KW) and ANOVA fail catastrophically; under moderate to strong spatial dependence, they reject the true null hypothesis over 94% of the time due to the unadjusted spatial variance inflation. The GLS method, while theoretically correct, suffered frequent convergence failures in our simulation and is omitted from the size and power tables. Table 2 illustrates the power of the test under location shift alternatives. While the test shows excellent power for independent data (omitted for brevity), its power under moderate (ϕ = 0.20) and strong (ϕ = 0.50) spatial dependence is heavily penalized. This reflects a fundamental statistical reality: strong spatial correlation drastically reduces the effective sample size of the dataset. The variance inflation is so substantial that small-to-moderate location shifts are masked by the natural spatial clustering, making them difficult to detect reliably without much larger spatial domains. Furthermore, at very strong dependence (ϕ = 0.50), the Satterthwaite approximation becomes highly conservative.

div.head: Multivariate Results
div.p: In the p = 2 multivariate simulation, testing equal mean vectors against a joint location shift alternative (δ = 0.15), the results strongly align with the univariate findings. As shown in Table 3, the Multivariate Kruskal-Wallis (with Bonferroni correction) and standard MANOVA exhibit severe Type I error inflation, rapidly approaching 100% under moderate and strong spatial correlation.

Conversely, the proposed Multivariate Spatial-CvM successfully maintains calibration under the null hypothesis (0.050 at ϕ = 0.01), effectively leveraging the exact 4p-dimensional discrete integration mapping to control false positive rates. Although it remains slightly conservative at higher spatial dependence (0.034 at ϕ = 0.50), this is a vast improvement over nonspatial parametric and non-parametric counterparts. Table 4 illustrates that while the test achieves substantial power for near-independent data (0.578), the heavy spatial variance inflation penalizes detectability as the spatial range increases.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This study validates a non-parametric spatial CvM testing framework for agricultural yield data. By combining kernel-smoothed EDFs with an exact discrete evaluation of the α-mixing spatial covariance, we offer a rigorously calibrated alternative to standard ANOVA and MANOVA tests, completely neutralizing the severe Type I error inflation inherently caused by spatial autocorrelation.
A Proof of Tightness (Detailed)
We prove tightness of { Gn,k } in ℓ ∞ (R) under the fixed-bandwidth infill design.
From the denominator expansion and the definition of Fk,h we obtain the linear form:
div.formula: Gn,k (x) = n k j=1 a n,j ξ kj (x) + r n (x), ξ kj (x) := 1{X k,s kj ≤ x} − F (x)
div.p: where the deterministic weights are a n,j := √ m n,k W j .
For x < y, define the centered increment variable η kj (x, y) := 1{X k,s kj ∈ (x, y]} − (F (y) − F (x)). Assume F is Lipschitz. By Davydov's inequality, for δ > 0:
div.formula: | Cov(η kj (x, y), η kl (x, y))| ≤ Cα(∥s kj − s kl ∥) δ/(2+δ) |y − x| 2/(2+δ)
div.p: Therefore, the second moment of the increment is bounded by:
div.formula: E     n k j=1 a n,j η kj (x, y)   2   ≤ C|y−x| 2/(2+δ) n k j,l=1 |a n,j a n,l |α(∥s kj −s kl ∥) δ/(2+δ)
div.p: Because K h is bounded and compactly supported, and utilizing the spatial mixing rate, the double sum over the lattice is uniformly bounded. There exists γ := 2/(2 + δ) > 0 such that E[( Gn,k (y) − Gn,k (x)) 2 ] ≤ C|y − x| γ + o(1). The increment moment bound, together with finitedimensional convergence, implies tightness of { Gn,k } in ℓ ∞ (R) by a standard moment criterion for tightness.
